transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-02-14
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~75 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam Patel (Redwood SE), Jorge Rivera (Orchard ML Eng), Priya Sinha (Orchard Infra), Evan Brooks (Orchard Product)

Summary: quick workshop to agree on how we'll run perf benchmarks to compare hosted vs dedicated vs on-prem. Focus on repeatability and avoiding apples-to-oranges comparisons.

[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, happy Valentines day, we'll try to keep this tight. Quick intro - I'm Maya, AE on the account, and Liam is our SE who runs the benchmark harness.
[00:18] Liam Patel: Hi all, Liam here. Agenda: sync on prompt sets, traffic shape, metrics that matter, and config matrix (batching, kv cache, quantization). We'll also go over how we instrument.
[00:36] Jorge Rivera: Great, thanks. High level, Orchard wants to validate latency SLOs and unit cost tradeoffs. We care about p95 and p99 tail, also throughput under steady-state and burst scenarios.
[00:52] Priya Sinha: From infra side, we need to make sure network variability is accounted for — on-prem vs hosted will have different egress and NIC behavior, we want to avoid blaming model runtime for network noise.
[01:07] Evan Brooks: Also want apples-to-apples for quantization experiments. If we compare int8 hosted vs int4 self-hosted, we need same prompt sets and same sampling config.
[01:25] Liam Patel: Exactly. First principle: keep everything equal except the variable under test. So same model weights, same tokenizer, same generation args (temperature/top_p/stop), same seed for sampling where applicable. Note: some runtime quantization paths require recompilation so we'll log kernel versions.
[01:46] Maya Chen: Quick question — Orchard, what are your canonical prompt sets? Are they short queries or long contexts?
[01:55] Jorge Rivera: We have three classes: short search-ish prompts (~16 tokens), medium multi-turn chat (~128 tokens), and long context summarization (~1024 tokens). We'll share examples.
[02:11] Liam Patel: Perfect. For benchmarking we typically provide a file with prompts and expected truncation lengths. We'll also provide a harness that can replay these with a target QPS distribution.
[02:24] Maya Chen: On the load generator, Liam mentioned k6 and a locust harness in the deck. Which do you recommend?
[02:33] Liam Patel: Both are fine. k6 is easier for high-concurrency HTTP load; Locust gives more flexibility for multi-step flows and user behavior. For apples-to-apples throughput we'd use k6 with fixed arrival rate and limited client-side batching to avoid client-induced consolidation.
[02:52] Jorge Rivera: Can you clarify client-side vs server-side batching? We saw some prior runs where client SDK did some automatic request coalescing and it inflated throughput numbers.
[03:03] Liam Patel: Good point — we must disable any client-side batching/caching. Server-side continuous batching is what we want to measure. We'll instrument batch sizes and per-batch latency.
[03:18] Priya Sinha: On the subject of KV cache, how do you recommend we measure cache hit rates and impact on latency?
[03:25] Liam Patel: We suggest three tests: cold-start (cache empty), warm-cache steady-state (simulate repeated prefixes to measure hit rate), and mixed workload with Pareto distribution of repeated prefixes. We'll log KV cache hit ratio, average batch size, and token-level latency.
[03:42] Evan Brooks: Is KV cache behavior deterministic across dedicated and hosted? I'm worried about eviction policies causing non-deterministic p99s.
[03:50] Liam Patel: Eviction policy is LRU-ish but heuristics can differ based on shard memory pressure. We'll capture cache size, eviction counts, and align memory allocation across setups as much as possible. For on-prem, we can pin cache size; for hosted we can request an equivalent config.
[04:07] Jorge Rivera: For quantization, we want to ensure parity in perplexity/quality. How do you measure that alongside perf?
[04:16] Liam Patel: We'll define a small held-out eval set from your prompt sets — run generation at identical sampling settings and compute BLEU/ROUGE/embedding similarity or human eval for a subset. We'll capture latency/cost for each quant level (fp16, int8, int4) and flag quality regressions.
[04:34] Maya Chen: Note: quantization can change kernel selection and memory layout; we'll include kernel and runtime version in every run artifact.
[04:43] Priya Sinha: What about sequence length distribution — throughput drops non-linearly as seq length increases. How do we account for that?
[04:51] Liam Patel: We'll stratify runs by seq-length bucket: short (<32), medium (32-256), long (256-1024). For each bucket we'll measure per-token throughput and token latency. We'll also report effective tokens/sec and tokens per GPU-second for cost analysis.
[05:10] Jorge Rivera: Regarding metrics, we want p50, p95, p99, p999 if possible, and tail latency plots over time. Also cpu/gpu utilization, memory, and NVMe I/O if applicable.
[05:22] Liam Patel: We'll collect Prometheus metrics for system counters and tracer spans for request level. The harness will emit per-request latencies so you can compute any percentile. Note: p999 requires a lot of samples — recommend long steady-state runs (30-60 mins) for valid tail estimates.
[05:41] Evan Brooks: How do you suggest we handle variability from autoscaling and warm-up effects?
[05:47] Liam Patel: We'll run a warmup phase (10-15 minutes) and then measurement window. For autoscaling configs we should fix the capacity (reserved) for apples-to-apples tests; otherwise autoscaling introduces confounding variables.
[06:03] Maya Chen: For dedicated vs hosted baseline, Redwood can provision a dedicated pool that matches the hosted instance type, and for on-prem we ask Orchard to match GPU type where possible or we run normalized per-GPU metrics.
[06:18] Priya Sinha: Network overheads: we will run both client and server in the same VPC for hosted tests to minimize egress noise; for on-prem we will run traffic inside our LAN. We'll record RTT distributions.
[06:32] Jorge Rivera: Can you talk about measurement of batching behavior? Specifically what traces we capture?
[06:38] Liam Patel: We'll capture batch size distribution, per-batch generation time, queueing delay (time waiting to be included in a batch), and per-request latency within batch. Also record fraction of requests that chart the batch boundaries.
[06:55] Speaker 2: Uh, and don't forget to log per-core GPU occupancy, kernel durations, and CUDA stream stalls — these help diagnose perf cliffs.
[07:07] Liam Patel: Yes good call. We'll include perf counters where available (NVIDIA DCGM, CUPTI traces) and attach flamegraphs for slow tails.
[07:20] Evan Brooks: For apples-to-apples cost comparisons, what's your recommended unit? Cost per 1M tokens served at p95 < X ms?
[07:29] Maya Chen: Typically teams look at cost per token at target p95/p99 thresholds and tokens per GPU-hour. We'll compute cost normalized to a reference region and instance SKU.
[07:39] Jorge Rivera: About reproducibility — how do we ensure the harness is deterministic enough to re-run?
[07:45] Liam Patel: We'll provide a harness with pinned dependencies and a results artifact (JSONL of requests/responses with timestamps, env dump, kernel/runtime versions). We'll store results in a shared S3 bucket or drive.
[07:58] Priya Sinha: Security and credentials: for on-prem runs we'll use a short-lived test token and a read-only role; we'll also need IP allowlist.
[08:08] Maya Chen: We'll send you a security checklist and a sandbox token procedure.
[08:15] Jorge Rivera: Okay, let's walk through a proposed minimal config matrix so we can agree: baseline (fp16, kv off, batch dynamic), kv enabled warm cache, int8 quant, int4 quant (if available), and on-prem run.
[08:31] Liam Patel: That sounds right. For each config, we run: 15 min warmup, 30 min steady-state, collecting per-request latencies, batch stats, cache metrics, and system counters.
[08:44] Evan Brooks: Will you also run a stress test with bursts to see how the system behaves under sudden traffic spikes?
[08:51] Liam Patel: Yes, we'll do a burst profile — ramp to 2-3x nominal QPS for 5 mins and observe latency and error rates. We'll also record queue growth and any fallback behavior.
[09:02] Maya Chen: A few gotchas from past benchmarks — make sure the model checkpoint matches across environments (sometimes a tokenization repo mismatch sneaks in), and match temperature and top_p.
[09:16] Jorge Rivera: Good note, we once had mismatch where hosted had a patched tokenizer and numbers were off.
[09:23] Priya Sinha: For on-prem resource accounting, we want to capture GPU power draw and host CPU load; can you accept those traces?
[09:30] Liam Patel: Yes, add NVML logs and node exporter metrics. We'll align timestamps and join traces post-run.
[09:39] Evan Brooks: Regarding data privacy, we'll scrub any PII from prompts before sharing results, agreed?
[09:44] Maya Chen: Absolutely — we'll provide a scrubbed dataset or run the eval inside your VPC if preferred.
[09:52] Jorge Rivera: Can we talk about how to compare different kernel/compile options? Sometimes an int4 path uses fused attention kernel which changes perf characteristics a lot.
[10:01] Liam Patel: We'll include kernel tags and compilation flags in run metadata. Also provide a note on which backend was used (XLA, Triton, custom kernel). That way you can filter runs by kernel.
[10:11] Maya Chen: I want to cover instrumentation of model quality. We'll capture embeddings for responses and compute cosine similarity to a baseline. For crucial prompts we may do manual spot checks.
[10:26] Jorge Rivera: For evaluation metrics, we'll include embedding sim, ROUGE for summarization, and for chat quality a small human-rated sample.
[10:33] Liam Patel: Ok, operationally, here's the plan we'll put in the runbook: share harness repo link, share prompt CSVs, share expected distro file (seq length histogram + arrival pattern), whitelist test IPs, run baseline hosted vs dedicated, then on-prem. We'll produce a single artifact with all runs and a summary sheet.
[10:52] Maya Chen: We'll attach our benchmark template spreadsheet and a short-run example.
[10:57] Evan Brooks: Can you share sample scripts for reproducing quantization builds? Our infra team wants the exact commands.
[11:03] Liam Patel: Yes, we'll include Dockerfiles and quantization scripts, including RNG seeds and compiler flags. Note: int4 may require custom kernels that aren't available in every build. We'll flag compatibility.
[11:16] Priya Sinha: Time sync — do you need our on-prem node access or will you run blackbox tests?
[11:22] Maya Chen: Ideally we run with an on-prem agent that you control (we provide the harness and you run it), but if you want Redwood to run we can negotiate secure access. For now, plan on you running the on-prem harness and sharing artifacts.
[11:38] Jorge Rivera: One more thing — what's your approach to statistical significance? If p95 differs by 10ms, is that meaningful?
[11:45] Liam Patel: We'll run multiple replicates and compute confidence intervals. For tail latencies, use bootstrapping to estimate CI. We'll flag differences that are outside the CI and show effect sizes.
[11:58] Maya Chen: Ok, quick recap and next steps: Maya to send harness + runbook; Liam to prepare config matrix and expected metrics spreadsheet; Orchard to provide prompts and traffic profile; schedule baseline run next week.
[12:12] Jorge Rivera: Sounds good. Any final questions?
[12:16] Evan Brooks: No more from me. Thanks.
[12:19] Priya Sinha: Thanks all.
[12:21] Maya Chen: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with calendar invites and links.

References/Artifacts mentioned:
- Benchmark harness repo: https://github.com/redwood-inference/benchmark-harness (shared privately)
- Prompt sets: orchard_prompts_3classes.csv (will be shared via drive)
- Benchmark template spreadsheet: https://redwood.app/benchmark-template (internal link)
- Security checklist and sandbox token doc (to be sent)

Closing notes: agreed methodology, expectation of shared artifacts by dates in action items.
